newsitem.title: USA: Testimony ends in Garcia Abrego trial.
newsitem.headline: Testimony ends in Garcia Abrego trial.

text.p: Testimony ended on Tuesday in the trial of accused drug kingpin Juan Garcia Abrego without his taking the stand in his own defence.
The defence rested its case after just three witnesses, setting the stage for closing arguments on Wednesday in a trial where much is at stake for the U.S. government.

Garcia Abrego, a former cookie factory worker from Texas, is accused of heading the Mexico-based Gulf cartel that authorities say at one time shipped up to a third of the cocaine consumed in the United States.

U.S. drug agents pursued Garcia Abrego for years and pressured Mexico to do the same. The United States made him a symbol of the fight against international drug-trafficking by placing him on the FBI's 10 Most Wanted list and has expended much time and energy on its attempt to convict him.
Garcia Abrego, 52, pleaded not guilty to 22 drug-related charges that could bring him life in prison, but his attorneys chose not to have him testify.

Instead, they put on three medical experts who gave sometimes conflicting testimony about whether Garcia Abrego was lucid when he told U.S. drug agents after his capture that he had smuggled pot and cocaine into the United States.
Garcia Abrego was caught in Monterrey, Mexico in January, after a former cartel insider tipped police to his whereabouts. He was flown to Houston for trial on U.S. indictments.

According to testimony, he told U.S. agents that he shipped up to 1,000 pounds (453 kilogram) of marijuana and 220 pounds (99.8 kilogram) of cocaine a month to the United States from his base in northern Mexico, but was not the major drug dealer that authorities claimed.

Mexican doctors gave him heart and blood pressure medicine and two tranquillisers -- Xanax and Valium -- before his two-hour flight to Houston, which defence attorneys said would have made him too high to give a credible statement upon arrival.

Medical reports read by defence witnesses said Garcia Abrego was dosed with the tranquillisers because he was in a state of high anxiety. Television reports at the time showed him struggling with Mexican police as they carried him to the jet waiting to take him to Houston.

Mexican doctors injected the then-portly Garcia Abrego with 20 milligrams of Valium. "Usually a human being of 160 to 170 pounds (74 to 77 kilogram) would have been rendered incapacitated and fallen asleep (with that dose)," forensic toxicologist Ernest Lykissa testified.

Agents who questioned Garcia Abrego and a doctor who examined him in Houston said he seemed sober at the time of the interrogation, but they had no videotape of the session nor did Garcia Abrego sign anything affirming his statement. Prosecutors said he had taken Valium for years to help him sleep and had developed a tolerance to the drug.

Prosecutors put on more than 50 witnesses in the first three weeks of the trial before resting their case on Monday. Their key testimony came from former cartel insiders who agreed to testify in exchange for reduced jail sentences or protection from the U.S. government.

They said Garcia Abrego led a vast, billion-dollar empire that shipped thousands of tonnes cocaine, often with the help of bribed officials in Mexico and the United States, and sometimes dealt in violence to eliminate wayward employees and others.

Defence attorneys attacked the credibility of the cartel members and pointed out that, despite years of wiretapping, the government recorded no phone call in which Garcia Abrego spoke or was mentioned by name.
The trial has been held under extremely tight security, with federal marshals ringing the courtroom at all times.
